clue.text: Sort of chap not expected to be in Murdoch book?

definitions.text: Sort of chap not expected to be in Murdoch book?

parts.words: Sort of chap not expected to be in Murdoch book?
parts.note: a man who turns up by chance, read as the title of an Iris Murdoch novel about such a man

explanation.surface: A reader wonders which kind of fellow would be a surprise in one of Iris Murdoch's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris Murdoch wrote the novel 'An Accidental Man'; the adjective in its title is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A chap nobody expected is one who arrives by chance, unplanned, as in Murdoch's title.

clue.text: Cleopatra's deliverers, like afterthought

parts.note: like and as both mean in the manner of
PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: Cleopatra's killers are mentioned in passing, like a postscript to her story.
explanation.walkthrough: Cleopatra killed herself with the bite of a venomous snake brought to her in a basket of figs, so the snakes delivered her from life.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says venomous Egyptian snakes ended Cleopatra's life, delivering her from captivity.

clue.text: Crime writer who made his mark

definitions.meaning: James M. ..., American author of The Postman Always Rings Twice
the Bible's first murderer, branded by God with a mark after killing his brother Abel

explanation.definitionFit: One surname covers the hard-boiled novelist and the biblical fratricide, whose sign marked him for life.

clue.text: Essay may be seen as sanitised rot

indicators.note: the phrase says these letters can be viewed as something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a student's essay as cleaned-up nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be seen as' tells you to rearrange SANITISED ROT, twelve letters that make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A long academic essay, such as one written for a degree, is this kind of treatise.

clue.text: Profit heard to accrue from human failing

indicators.note: a failing thing breaks down, so the letters of human collapse into a new order

explanation.surface: Gains are said to come out of people's weaknesses.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works by sound: 'Profit heard' is 'prophet', and Nahum is a minor prophet of the Old Testament. 'failing' rearranges HUMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoken aloud, profit becomes prophet, and this book of the Bible carries the name of one such seer.

clue.text: Secret things books left out

definitions.meaning: the Greek source word means hidden things
writings excluded from the accepted canon of the Bible

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek word means hidden matters, and it names scripture kept out of the canon.

clue.text: University men like Lyly and Marlowe had theirs about them

definitions.text: University men like Lyly and Marlowe had theirs about them

parts.words: University men like Lyly and Marlowe had theirs about them
parts.note: the group name of Elizabethan playwrights educated at Oxford and Cambridge, plus the idiom for being alert

explanation.surface: Elizabethan writers educated at the universities kept their minds sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: Lyly, Marlowe, Greene and Peele are called the University Wits; to have your wits about you is to stay alert.
explanation.definitionFit: The University Wits were these playwrights' group label, and sharp minds are what someone alert keeps about them.

clue.text: Titian is, or may be seen as, among Venetian School ones

indicators.note: the phrase says these words can be viewed in another form, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Titian is counted among the founders of the Venetian school of painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be seen as' rearranges TITIAN IS OR; the surface statement about Titian is also true.
explanation.definitionFit: Titian ranks among the founders who started the Venetian school, so he is one of its originators.

clue.text: Tennyson has them "whirling their sabres in circles of light"

definitions.text: Tennyson has them "whirling their sabres in circles of light"

parts.words: Tennyson has them "whirling their sabres in circles of light"
parts.note: a line from Tennyson's poem The Charge of the Heavy Brigade, about a Scottish cavalry regiment

explanation.surface: A quotation from Tennyson about cavalrymen whirling their swords.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Charge of the Heavy Brigade, Tennyson describes the Scottish dragoon regiment riding grey horses at Balaclava.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Scots Greys were a British cavalry regiment, named for their grey horses, that charged at Balaclava.

clue.text: "Oh, why has — privilege to lie? / And yet to be believed!" (Dryden, Oedipus)

definitions.text: "Oh, why has — privilege to lie? / And yet to be believed!" (Dryden, Oedipus)

parts.words: "Oh, why has — privilege to lie? / And yet to be believed!" (Dryden, Oedipus)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing words are the clergy as a body, from Dryden and Lee's Oedipus

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dryden's Oedipus complaining that some may lie and still be believed.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the dash from the line in Dryden's Oedipus attacking the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: The order of priests, the clergy as a body, is the group the speaker accuses of lying.

clue.text: African Queen performed complete circle

parts.note: did means carried out or performed
the letter O is round like a full circle

explanation.surface: A film title, The African Queen, seems to be performing a full turn.
explanation.walkthrough: Dido was the legendary founder and queen of Carthage, in North Africa; the surface evokes the film The African Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido founded Carthage in North Africa and ruled it as its queen.

clue.text: Bereft by Berryman

definitions.meaning: stripped of one's property or home

explanation.definitionFit: Someone bereft has been deprived, and The Dispossessed is a book of poems by John Berryman.

clue.text: She was "brave as Margaret Queen / And tall as Amazon"

definitions.text: She was "brave as Margaret Queen / And tall as Amazon"

parts.words: She was "brave as Margaret Queen / And tall as Amazon"
parts.note: lines from Keats's poem about the gypsy woman of Scott's novel Guy Mannering

explanation.surface: A quotation describing a woman as brave as a queen and tall as an Amazon.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats wrote a ballad on the gypsy of Scott's Guy Mannering; these lines close it.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's ballad celebrates this gypsy heroine of Scott's Guy Mannering, a tall and fearless woman.

clue.text: "It's so nice to meet a man who isn't — about catching my beri-beri " (Dorothy Parker)

definitions.text: "It's so nice to meet a man who isn't — about catching my beri-beri " (Dorothy Parker)

parts.words: "It's so nice to meet a man who isn't — about catching my beri-beri " (Dorothy Parker)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word is the childish name for a timid person

explanation.surface: A Dorothy Parker line praising a man who isn't frightened of catching her illness.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the dash with the playground word for a coward.
explanation.definitionFit: Children call a timid, easily frightened person by this name, and Parker's man is not afraid of infection.

clue.text: Leading players in Banjo Paterson's bush

definitions.text: Leading players in Banjo Paterson's bush

parts.words: Leading players in Banjo Paterson's bush
parts.note: the people of the Australian back country, who are the main figures in Banjo Paterson's ballads

explanation.surface: Who were the stars in the outback verse of the Australian poet Banjo Paterson?
explanation.walkthrough: Banjo Paterson, author of Waltzing Matilda, wrote ballads about the Australian bush, known as the outback.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of the Australian back country are the drovers and stockmen who star in Paterson's bush ballads.

clue.text: Miles off target with surrogate in this

definitions.text: Miles off target with surrogate in this

parts.words: Miles off target with surrogate in this
parts.note: Longfellow's Miles Standish sends a friend to woo for him, and misses the mark

explanation.surface: Someone is miles away from their goal after using a stand-in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miles' is not a distance but Miles Standish of Longfellow's poem The Courtship of Miles Standish, who sends John Alden to propose for him; Priscilla prefers Alden.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooing is what Standish attempts through a go-between, giving Longfellow's poem its title.

clue.text: Memorial for Dickens's would-be homicidal schoolmaster

definitions.meaning: a gravestone marks and commemorates a burial
Bradley, the teacher in Our Mutual Friend who tries to kill Eugene Wrayburn

explanation.definitionFit: A grave marker is a memorial, and it is also the surname of the murderous teacher in Our Mutual Friend.

clue.text: Pre-Raphaelite father figure?

definitions.meaning: Walter ..., the Victorian critic linked to the Pre-Raphaelite and aesthetic circle
the Latin word for father, used in old-fashioned British slang

explanation.definitionFit: Walter Pater belonged to the aesthetic circle around the Pre-Raphaelites, and his surname is Latin for a father.

clue.text: Asimov character seen to steal book

parts.note: to rob is to steal from
OT, the Old Testament, is a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A character from Isaac Asimov is spotted stealing a volume.
explanation.walkthrough: Isaac Asimov wrote I, Robot; his stories are full of mechanical characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Asimov's science fiction is peopled with mechanical men, as in I, Robot.

clue.text: Pedestrian work by Bridges?

definitions.meaning: a poem by Robert Bridges, Poet Laureate, about a ship sailing by

explanation.definitionFit: Someone walking by is a pedestrian, and Robert Bridges wrote a poem with this title.

clue.text: Jamesian father with a leaning, clearly, toward bitterness

definitions.text: Jamesian father with a leaning, clearly, toward bitterness

parts.words: Jamesian father with a leaning, clearly, toward bitterness
parts.note: the cold, sardonic physician father in Henry James's Washington Square, whose surname suggests something that slopes

explanation.surface: A father in a Henry James novel is described as inclined to be sour.
explanation.walkthrough: In Washington Square the heroine Catherine's father is a doctor; his surname read literally is one with a leaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James made Catherine's sardonic physician father the antagonist of Washington Square.

clue.text: All-round overview of Italian language

parts.note: the round letter O
a scan is a quick survey or overview

explanation.surface: Someone takes a full survey of a language spoken in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscan was an ancient language of southern Italy, related to Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: This extinct tongue was spoken in ancient southern Italy, close kin to Latin.

clue.text: Secure playwright

definitions.meaning: to fasten a door with a sliding bar
Robert ..., author of A Man for All Seasons

explanation.definitionFit: Fastening a door with a bar secures it, and Robert Bolt wrote A Man for All Seasons.

clue.text: Persian ally gets audible reward

indicators.note: audible signals that the word for reward is spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: meed is an old word for a reward

explanation.surface: An ally of Persia receives a prize that everyone can hear.
explanation.walkthrough: The Medes and Persians were allied peoples of the ancient Near East.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Medes were joined with the Persians in one empire, so one of them was a Persian's ally.

clue.text: Figured lace for Durrell girl

indicators.note: figured means worked into a pattern, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Patterned lace makes a present for a girl in a Durrell novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figured' rearranges LACE; the title character of the last book of Lawrence Durrell's Alexandria Quartet is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence Durrell named the final novel of his Alexandria Quartet after this woman painter.

clue.text: Edith Wharton's gift from the grave

definitions.text: Edith Wharton's gift from the grave

parts.words: Edith Wharton's gift from the grave
parts.note: the title of Edith Wharton's novella, in which a man profits by publishing a dead woman's love letters

explanation.surface: A present left by Edith Wharton after her death.
explanation.walkthrough: In Wharton's novella The Touchstone, Glennard sells the letters of a dead novelist who loved him; they are his gift from the grave.
explanation.definitionFit: Wharton titled the novella after a test of true worth, which the dead writer's letters become for Glennard.

clue.text: The work by Cowper

definitions.meaning: a job or piece of work to be done
William Cowper's long blank-verse poem of 1785

explanation.definitionFit: A piece of work set to be done is a chore, and William Cowper wrote a long poem with this title.

clue.text: "And Blucher, prompt and prow, / And Jean the Crown Prince" (Hardy, Leipzig)

definitions.text: "And Blucher, prompt and prow, / And Jean the Crown Prince" (Hardy, Leipzig)

parts.words: "And Blucher, prompt and prow, / And Jean the Crown Prince" (Hardy, Leipzig)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word is the surname of the French marshal who became Crown Prince of Sweden

explanation.surface: Lines from Hardy's poem Leipzig naming generals who fought Napoleon.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy's line ends with the surname of Jean-Baptiste, the French marshal adopted as Crown Prince of Sweden who fought Napoleon at Leipzig in 1813.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Baptiste, Napoleon's former marshal, became Crown Prince of Sweden and led an allied army at Leipzig.
